Reproducing Kim et al. (2023) from dandiset 000633¶

Paper. Kim V, Semenov I, Kiester AS, Keppler MA, Ibey BL, Bixler JN, Colunga Biancatelli RML, Pakhomov AG (2023). Control of the electroporation efficiency of nanosecond pulses by swinging the electric field vector direction. Int. J. Mol. Sci. 24, 10921. doi:10.3390/ijms241310921.

Claims file. claims/000633/10.3390-ijms241310921.yaml, written from the version of record (open access, Europe PMC PMC10341945). The paper has no supplement and links no code.

Dandiset. DANDI:000633, version 0.231013.2226. The paper cites no version of the dandiset. This is the only published version, and the most recent; the draft lists the same two assets with the same sizes and was last modified when this version was published (2023-10-13), so the two do not differ in anything the analysis uses.

What the dandiset holds. Two NWB files, each one stitched whole-dish fluorescence image of a BPAE cell monolayer in two channels (MemBrite and YO-PRO-1): Single-pulse_trains and Paired-pulse_trains. The dandiset's title is the legend of Figure 4 ("The difference in electroporation patterns produced by a train of single pulses and a train of paired pulses"), so these are taken as the images of Figure 4A (single pulses) and Figure 4B (paired pulses). The session description of the single-pulse file describes another exposure (see the data check), so this identification rests on the file names, the dandiset's title and the images themselves (three electrodes in a triangle, uptake around one base electrode), and both Figure 4 outcomes rest on it. The ROI measurements of Figure 2 (n = 3 at each of 1 Hz and 833 kHz), the square-array experiments of Figure 3 and the strobe imaging of Figure 5 are not in it.

Outside inputs. None. Two claims need the electric field map of the paper's Sim4Life simulation (Methods 4.3), which is not deposited. It is computed here from the geometry the paper states and the electrode positions measured in the images (see swing.py); this substitutes for the paper's solver and is recorded as a deviation.

For the Figure 2 claims, a section near the end computes, for information only, the 833 kHz angle curve that the two Figure 4 images allow (one dish each, not the paper's n = 3, and no 1 Hz data). It decides no outcome.

import time
import warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from scipy.ndimage import median_filter, uniform_filter

import swing

pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)

started = time.time()
assets = swing.assets()
meta, img = {}, {}
for a in assets:
    m, im = swing.load_binned(a["url"])
    m["path"], m["size"], m["url"] = a["path"], a["size"], a["url"]
    meta[m["session_id"]], img[m["session_id"]] = m, im
SINGLE, PAIRED = "Single-pulse_trains", "Paired-pulse_trains"
print(f"dandiset {swing.DANDISET_ID} version {swing.DANDISET_VERSION}: {len(assets)} files streamed "
      f"in {time.time() - started:.0f} s, binned {swing.BIN} x {swing.BIN}")

  session_description: In this experimental setup, a cell monolayer is subjected to a train of electrical pulses, delivered through a triangular electrode array where two base electrodes are connected to two separate channels. The innovative design ensures that as one channel is energized, the other is automatically grounded, and vice versa. This dynamic allows for the efficient electroporation of the cells with a train of 5 paired-pulses, each consisting of a 600+600 ns duration. The application occurs at a frequency of 833 kHz and an amplitude of 2 kV, ensuring precise and controlled exposure.

image description (same in both files): IX83 microscope used; MS-2000 scanning stage; X-Cite 110LED illuminator; ORCA-Flash4 sCMOS camera;CellSens software for automation; Channel 1 ex/em 350/460nm for MemBrite dye; ex/em 480/535nm for YOPRO-1; dark circles indicate electrode footprints; 144 images captured in a 12x12 grid from a six-well plate; 216 additional images with DAPI and FITC filter cubes; all images automatically stitched for a final composite; 10×, 0.38NA objective used for high-resolution imaging.

The image is stored as an ImageSeries of shape (22323, 22323, 2) with a rate of 2 Hz. NWB reads the first axis of an ImageSeries as time, so a standard reader sees 22323 frames of 22323 x 2 pixels; the data are one image of 22323 x 22323 pixels in two channels, as the description of stitched tiles says. No pixel size, channel names or intensity unit (n.a.) are stored; the channel order comes only from the free-text description (MemBrite listed first, then YO-PRO-1), and is checked below. About 16% of pixels are exactly zero in every channel: the corners outside the scanned tiles.

The session description of Single-pulse_trains describes another experiment: "4 co-directional paired-pulse (600 + 600 ns) trains ... 770 kHz, amplitude 10 kV/cm", which are the settings of Figure 3 (Section 2.2; there, a square array of four electrodes). The image shows three electrode footprints in a triangle (below), as in Figure 4A, and its uptake lies around one base electrode, as in Figure 4A. The file is taken as Figure 4A from its name, the dandiset's title and this layout; the description contradicts it, and nothing in the data can settle which exposure the image records. Figure 4A is five single 600 ns pulses at 833 kHz and 4 kV; if the image were instead four co-directional pairs at 770 kHz, it would be an exposure in which "the electric field direction stayed the same in each pair", as the description says. The description does not say which electrodes were energized; that the field came from one base electrode is an inference from the uptake around one of them. The tests of fig4a and fig4bc rest on this identification. The Paired-pulse_trains description gives an amplitude of 2 kV, while the paper gives 4 kV for both Figure 4 images (Section 2.3); the field check below bears on this. The description mentions a six-well plate; the paper used 35 mm glass-bottom dishes (Methods 4.1). Subject age is "P1D" for a cell line, and each "subject" is a condition, not an animal.

Both images show three dark footprints in an isosceles triangle with a base of 4.6 to 4.7 mm and sides of 6.6 to 6.8 mm, so the two dishes used the same array, turned about 180 degrees between them. The scale set from the 1.5 mm needle (Methods 4.2) is 0.654 um per pixel, which is what the camera and objective named in the file give (6.5 um / 10 = 0.65 um), and makes the image 14.6 mm wide, about the size of a 14 mm glass window. The scale is consistent with the data, not shown by them. Footprints are dark in channel 1, where cells under the needle were shielded from the field and took up no dye (ratio 0.68 and 0.81), and not in channel 0 (0.99 and 1.03); channel 1 is YO-PRO-1 and channel 0 MemBrite, as the description lists them. The two images are distinct recordings (different footprint positions, low pixel correlation), so neither is deposited twice. They are still images: there are no time series or trial tables whose clocks need to agree.

# The field model (swing.solve_potential): 2D conduction between three 1.5 mm electrodes in a 35 mm dish.
field = {}
for s in (SINGLE, PAIRED):
    e = E[s]
    els = [(f["x"] * um, f["y"] * um) for f in (e["apex"], e["base_a"], e["base_b"])]
    ny, nx = img[s][1].shape
    t0 = time.time()
    origin, h, phi = swing.solve_potential(els, [[0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]], (nx / 2 * um, ny / 2 * um))
    field[s] = {"origin": origin, "h": h, "phi": phi}
    for k in range(2):
        ex, ey = swing.field_from_potential(phi[k], h)
        field[s][f"e{k}"] = (ex, ey)
        field[s][f"mag{k}"] = np.hypot(ex, ey) * 1e4          # V/cm per volt applied
    print(f"{s}: solved on a {phi.shape[1]} x {phi.shape[2]} grid of {h:.0f} um in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

# The paper's field along the bisecting line (Section 2.1: 5 to 10 kV/cm) against the amplitude.
e = E[PAIRED]
bx, by, bd = swing.bisector_points(e["apex"], (e["base_a"], e["base_b"]), um)
mag_b = swing.sample(field[PAIRED]["mag0"], field[PAIRED]["origin"], field[PAIRED]["h"], bx * um, by * um)
print(f"\nField on the bisecting line of the paired-pulse dish, {len(bd)} points from the base midpoint to the apex footprint:")
for volts in (4000, 2000):
    print(f"  at {volts / 1000:.0f} kV: {mag_b.min() * volts / 1000:.1f} to {mag_b.max() * volts / 1000:.1f} kV/cm")

# Grid check: the same solve on a 60 um grid.
els = [(f["x"] * um, f["y"] * um) for f in (e["apex"], e["base_a"], e["base_b"])]
ny, nx = img[PAIRED][1].shape
o60, h60, phi60 = swing.solve_potential(els, [[0, 1, 0]], (nx / 2 * um, ny / 2 * um), h=60.0)
ex60, ey60 = swing.field_from_potential(phi60[0], h60)
m60 = swing.sample(np.hypot(ex60, ey60) * 1e4, o60, h60, bx * um, by * um)
print(f"  60 um grid against 40 um grid on the bisecting line: largest relative difference {np.max(np.abs(m60 / mag_b - 1)):.3f}")

Paired-pulse_trains: solved on a 878 x 878 grid of 40 um in 8 s

Field on the bisecting line of the paired-pulse dish, 27 points from the base midpoint to the apex footprint:
  at 4 kV: 4.2 to 9.7 kV/cm
  at 2 kV: 2.1 to 4.8 kV/cm

With the 4 kV of Section 2.3, the computed field on the bisecting line runs from about 4 to 10 kV/cm, close to the "5 to 10 kV/cm" Section 2.1 gives for this array; with the 2 kV of the file's description it would be 2 to 5 kV/cm. This is consistent with the paper's amplitude, not a proof of it: the field model is computed here, not measured. The solve changes little with the grid.

In the single-pulse image the footprints have soft edges and fit to smaller circles (1.03 to 1.40 mm, edge s.d. 128 to 144 um, against 1.47 to 1.52 mm and 33 to 99 um in the paired-pulse image). Only the fitted centres are used: every ROI is placed from a 750 um radius around the fitted centre, the needle's own radius. The views above show whether the centres sit in the middle of the dark discs.

fig4a-single-pulse-follows-field¶

Under a train of five single pulses applied to one base electrode (833 kHz, 4 kV), YP uptake is distributed as the electric field strength map.

Criterion (claims file): background-subtracted YP in 200 x 200 um ROIs over the image (footprint background, Methods 4.4), compared with the field in the same ROIs by (a) Spearman rank correlation or (b) the order of the three electrode neighbourhoods by YP matching their order by field. Reproduced when both agree with the map (correlation positive with p < 0.05, and the same order).

The field map is computed here (see the data check), for a single pulse on one base electrode with the other two grounded (Methods 4.2), scaled to 4 kV. Which base electrode is E1, the one pulsed, is not in the file, and the paper's text does not give its place: the Figure 4 legend says only that the panels are shown "with electrode positions labeled" and that E1 is the electrode pulsed in A. The published panel A has the apex at the top and E1 at the lower right, and so does the deposited image (the data check prints the apex position), but the registry's checks keep a published figure out of the notebook, so that placement is not shown here; and the deposited images do not keep one orientation (the paired-pulse image has its apex at the bottom). E1 is taken as base_a, the lower-right base electrode, which is also the base electrode with the most uptake (with E1 = base_b, the grounded electrode would show 2.5 times the uptake of the pulsed one). Both assignments are run. The neighbourhood of an electrode is taken as the ROIs whose centre lies within 500 um of its footprint edge (the claims file does not fix it; 250 and 1000 um are shown too, with the neighbourhood means for each). The ROI grid covers the image within 6 mm of its centre, leaving out ROIs whose centre is within 150 um of a footprint edge; the effect of both choices is shown. Contiguous ROIs are not independent, so the p-value of the full grid is far too small; the correlation is also tested on ROIs thinned to 1 mm and 2 mm spacing.

e = E[s]
yp = img[s][1].astype(float)
bg, bg_each = swing.background(yp, fps[s], 750 / um)
ypb = yp - bg
print(f"Footprint background: {bg:.1f} (per footprint {np.round(bg_each, 1).tolist()}); dish median {np.median(yp[yp > 0]):.1f}")
names = ["apex", "base_a", "base_b"]
assign = {"E1 = base_a (lower right)": 0, "E1 = base_b (lower left)": 1}
short = {0: "base_a", 1: "base_b"}

def fig4a_measure(radius_um, margin_um, ring_um, k):
    cen = swing.roi_grid(yp.shape, fps[s], um, radius_um, margin_um)
    Y = np.array([swing.roi_mean(ypb, x, y, swing.ROI_UM / um) for x, y in cen])
    F = swing.roi_field(field[s][f"mag{k}"] * 4000 / 1000, field[s]["origin"], field[s]["h"], cen, um)  # kV/cm
    rho, p = stats.spearmanr(F, Y)
    thin = {}
    for step in (1000, 2000):
        i = swing.thin_rois(cen, um, step)
        thin[step] = (len(i), *stats.spearmanr(F[i], Y[i]))
    neigh = []
    for n in names:
        f = e[n]
        d = np.hypot(cen[:, 0] - f["x"], cen[:, 1] - f["y"]) * um
        m = d < 750 + ring_um
        neigh.append((n, Y[m].mean(), F[m].mean(), int(m.sum())))
    order_yp = [x[0] for x in sorted(neigh, key=lambda t: -t[1])]
    order_f = [x[0] for x in sorted(neigh, key=lambda t: -t[2])]
    return len(cen), rho, p, neigh, order_yp, order_f, thin

rows = []
for label, k in assign.items():
    n, rho, p, neigh, oy, of, thin = fig4a_measure(6000, 150, 500, k)
    print(f"\n{label}: {n} ROIs, Spearman rho = {rho:.3f}, p = {p:.2g}")
    for step, (nt, rt, pt) in thin.items():
        print(f"   thinned to {step / 1000:.0f} mm spacing: {nt} ROIs, rho = {rt:.3f}, p = {pt:.2g}")
    for name, y, fld, cnt in neigh:
        print(f"   {name:7s} neighbourhood (0-500 um): {cnt} ROIs, mean YP above background {y:7.1f}, mean field {fld:5.2f} kV/cm")
    print(f"   order by YP: {oy}; order by field: {of}; same order: {oy == of}")
    for radius in (5000, 6000):
        for margin in (150, 400):
            for ring in (250, 500, 1000):
                if ring <= margin:
                    continue  # no ROI centre lies between the margin and the neighbourhood's outer edge
                n2, r2, p2, ng2, oy2, of2, th2 = fig4a_measure(radius, margin, ring, k)
                rows.append({"E1": short[k], "grid_radius_mm": radius / 1000, "margin_um": margin, "neighbourhood_um": ring,
                             "rois": n2, "spearman_rho": round(r2, 3), "p": float(f"{p2:.2g}"),

Result: reproduced, resting on the assumption that E1 is base_a, the lower-right base electrode, and that this file is the image of Figure 4A. With E1 = base_a, YP and the computed field are rank-correlated over 2627 ROIs (rho = 0.666), and the correlation holds on ROIs thinned to 1 mm spacing (rho = 0.666, p = 9.3e-15, 105 ROIs) and to 2 mm (rho = 0.654, p = 0.00053, 24 ROIs). The three neighbourhoods have the same order by YP and by field (base_a 649.8, base_b 262.6, apex 82.2 above background; 12.88, 7.38 and 5.31 kV/cm). Across grid radius, margin and neighbourhood width (250, 500 and 1000 um), rho is 0.640 to 0.746 and the order always matches; thinned to 1 mm, p is 2.7e-8 or less; thinned to 2 mm, p is below 0.05 in 8 of 10 variants and 0.095 in the two with a 5 mm grid and a 400 um margin, where only 12 ROIs are left. With E1 = base_b the correlation is weaker (0.424 to 0.510; 0.397 to 0.643 at 2 mm spacing, p up to 0.054) and the order differs in every variant, so the criterion's two readings would disagree. Where Figure 4A places E1 cannot be shown in this notebook, and the deposited images do not keep one orientation, so the assignment rests in the end on the uptake: E1 is the base electrode with the most uptake. That is the same direction the test checks, so the order reading (b) is not an independent check of the assignment; the correlation reading (a) is positive under both assignments. The outcome also rests on this file being the image of Figure 4A, which its session description contradicts (data check).

fig4bc-paired-pulse-focal-apex¶

Under five paired pulses applied to the two base electrodes in alternation (833 kHz, 4 kV), electroporation is strong near the grounded apex electrode and weak or absent near the base electrodes, despite the strong field there.

Criterion (claims file): background-subtracted YP in 200 x 200 um ROIs centred (a) 100 um and (b) 500 um outside the edge of each footprint, on the line from that electrode toward the array centre. Reproduced when, under both readings, YP near the apex in the paired-pulse image exceeds that near each base electrode, and the ratio of apex to base YP is higher in the paired-pulse image than in the single-pulse image. The array centre is taken as the centroid of the three electrode centres. The footprint edge is 750 um from the fitted centre (Methods 4.2).

Result: reproduced, resting on the assumption that the single-pulse file is the image of Figure 4A. Under both readings, YP near the apex in the paired-pulse image is above YP near each base electrode (2.7 to 8.1 times, from the table), and the apex-to-base ratios are far higher in the paired-pulse image than in the single-pulse image, where the apex neighbourhood has the least uptake (ratios 0.05 to 0.20). The computed field near the base electrodes during the pulse on that electrode is higher than near the apex, as the claim says ("despite the strong field there"). The single-pulse half of the contrast rests on the file being the image of Figure 4A (data check). The exposure its description gives instead is four co-directional pairs, in which "the electric field direction stayed the same in each pair"; it does not say which electrodes were energized, and that the field came from one base electrode is an inference from the uptake around one of them.

fig4-comet-shape¶

Under paired pulses the electroporated cells form a comet-shaped region pointing from the apex electrode towards the base.

Criterion (claims file): the electroporated region is background-subtracted YP above (a) half and (b) a quarter of its maximum in the paired-pulse image, after smoothing over 200 x 200 um. Reproduced when, under both readings, the region touches the apex footprint and extends further along the bisecting line toward the base than across it.

The region is the set of connected pixels above threshold that touch the apex footprint (swing.comet_region), inside 6 mm of the image centre and outside the footprints. The 200 um mean is taken over the pixels inside that area only (swing.masked_mean_filter), so the dark footprints and image corners do not lower the values next to them. "Further toward the base than across" is measured from the apex centre: the reach along the bisecting line toward the base against the largest distance across it, on either side. The extents along and across the line are shown too. How the maximum is taken matters (below): the literal maximum of the 200 um mean lies on one object far brighter than anything else in the dish. That object is shown at full resolution in both channels. Four versions are run: the literal maximum of the 200 um mean; the literal maximum of the 200 um mean after leaving out objects that are bright in the MemBrite channel (swing.debris_mask; MemBrite stains all cell membranes about evenly, so an object many times brighter than the monolayer in it is not a monolayer cell; thresholds of 5, 10 and 20 times the dish median); the 99.5th percentile of the 200 um mean; and the maximum of a 200 um median filter.

Grey scale 0 to the maximum of each version; values above it are shown at the top of the scale.

Result: reproduced, resting on the assumption that objects bright in the MemBrite channel are not part of the electroporated monolayer. The literal maximum of the 200 um mean (3999) lies on one object 2468 um from the apex: at full resolution it is a blurred disc about 105 um across (8688 um2), bright in both channels (YP median 14577 and MemBrite median 5266, against 305 and 255 around it), larger than a cell and out of focus, so likely debris above the monolayer. With that maximum, the region at half and at a quarter of it is empty, and the claim fails under both readings. Leaving out the objects whose MemBrite is above 10 times the dish median (0.54% of the region), the literal maximum of the 200 um mean is 1063, 1063 um from the apex, and the region touches the apex footprint and reaches further toward the base than across the line at half (1755 against 1315 um) and at a quarter (3929 against 1749 um); thresholds of 5 and 20 times give the same. The 99.5th percentile of the 200 um mean (half, 2935 against 1607 um; quarter, 4127 against 2269 um) and the maximum of a 200 um median filter (2603 against 1248; 4002 against 2064) agree. In every version with a region, it reaches less far away from the base than toward it and touches neither base footprint.

The pass rests on the measure: the reach from the apex centre along the bisecting line toward the base, against the largest distance across the line. The full extents of the region do not always agree with it. At half maximum, in the versions without bright objects, on which the outcome rests, the extent along the line is smaller than the extent across it (2446 against 2592 um at 10 and 20 times, 2446 against 2473 um at 5 times), and the region is a blob around the apex footprint about as wide as it is long (map above). The extents agree with the reach at a quarter maximum (5218 against 3368 um) and in the 99.5th-percentile and median-filter versions (half maximum, 4160 against 3038 and 3195 against 1750 um). The rule leaves out every binned pixel above the MemBrite threshold, 0.54% of the region at 10 times (1.50% at 5 times), which is several objects, not only the one under the literal maximum; the maximum without them (1063) is also the highest value outside 500 um of that object.

Figure 2 at 833 kHz from the Figure 4 images (for information; decides no outcome)¶

The Figure 2 claims need the ROI data of Figure 2: three experiments at each of 1 Hz and 833 kHz. They are not in the dandiset, and the four Figure 2 claims are blocked. The two Figure 4 images are one dish each of five single 600 ns pulses and of five paired pulses at 833 kHz in the same array, so they allow one 833 kHz curve with n = 1, if they were made in the way of Section 2.1. The paper does not say they were. The curve is computed as Section 2.1 describes, for information: contiguous 200 um ROIs on the bisecting line from the base midpoint to the apex footprint, YP above the footprint background, the paired-pulse value as % of the single-pulse value at the same distance from the base midpoint, and the angle between the field vectors of the two pulses of a pair from the computed field. The paper's 32 ROIs do not fit on this line (5.5 mm, 27 ROIs).

These numbers come from one pair of dishes that the paper presents as Figure 4, not from the Figure 2 experiments, and they decide no outcome. Near the base the single-pulse YP is high and the ratio is stable; toward the apex the single-pulse YP falls close to the footprint background, so the ratio there swings widely from one ROI to the next.

Blocked claims¶

  • fig2-cancellation-at-180, fig2-crossover-angle, fig2-facilitation-plateau, fig2-60-fold-co-counter: data missing. The 32-ROI measurements of Figure 2, three experiments at each of 1 Hz and 833 kHz, are not in the dandiset; there are no 1 Hz images at all. The Sim4Life field simulation that gives each ROI's angle is not deposited either.
  • fig3-1hz-co-cross-same, fig3-770khz-co-enhanced, fig3-770khz-cross-same-as-1hz: data missing. No image from the square four-electrode array of Figure 3 is in the dandiset (both images show three footprints).
  • fig5-base-sawtooth, fig5-apex-larger-polarization: data missing. The strobe images of FluoVolt-loaded CHO cells are not in the dandiset.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The field map is computed here by a two-dimensional finite-difference solve, in place of the paper's Sim4Life model; the electrode positions are measured in the images and the scale is set from the 1.5 mm needles. The measures for the image-only findings of Figure 4 are the claims file's readings, as the paper gives none. The single-pulse file is taken as Figure 4A although its session description gives other settings, and E1 as its lower-right base electrode, which is also the one with the most uptake; where Figure 4A places E1 is not shown here. For the comet shape, the pixels on objects bright in MemBrite (0.54% of the region, several objects, among them the one under the literal maximum, likely debris) are left out before the maximum is taken; with them, the half- and quarter-maximum regions are empty. The comet passes by the reach along the bisecting line against the distance across it; at half maximum the full extent of the region along the line is smaller than across it.

What was found about the dataset. It holds only the two images of Figure 4; the data behind Figures 2, 3 and 5, on which the paper's quantitative findings rest, are not deposited. The image is stored as an ImageSeries whose first axis NWB reads as time, with no pixel size, channel names or intensity unit. The session description of the single-pulse file gives the settings of a Figure 3 experiment (co-directional pairs, 770 kHz, 10 kV/cm), and that of the paired-pulse file an amplitude of 2 kV where the paper gives 4 kV. The file does not say which base electrode is E1. One object about 105 um across, bright in both channels, holds the brightest YP in the paired-pulse image.
